analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to cover proven preventive care for chronic conditions with no copay.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees in July 2021 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend three federal laws so that group health plans and insurers must cover certain preventive services for people with chronic conditions — at minimum heart disease, diabetes, osteoporosis, hypertension, asthma, liver disease, bleeding disorders, and depression — with no copays, deductibles, or other cost sharing. The services must be low-cost and backed by clinical evidence that they prevent conditions from getting worse or causing costlier secondary illnesses. The bill also allowed high-deductible health plans to keep paying for these services without affecting Health Savings Account eligibility.
analysis.who_benefits: People living with chronic conditions such as diabetes, heart disease, asthma, hypertension, and depression would get recommended preventive services and screenings free of charge, removing the upfront cost that often causes people to skip care until their condition worsens.

how_it_helps.text: Requires group health plans and insurers to cover additional preventive care and screenings for people with chronic conditions without any cost sharing, on top of existing free-preventive-care rules under the Affordable Care Act.

At minimum covers eight conditions: heart disease, diabetes, osteoporosis and osteopenia, hypertension, asthma, liver disease, bleeding disorders, and depression, with the list reviewable and expandable by the Health and Human Services Secretary every three years.

Limits the required coverage to low-cost items and services with clinical evidence they prevent an exacerbation of the chronic condition or a costlier secondary condition, targeting cases where a small upfront cost avoids a large later one.
Amends the Internal Revenue Code so that high-deductible health plans can pay for this preventive care without disqualifying holders from contributing to Health Savings Accounts.

analysis.who_pays: Insurers and employers sponsoring group health plans would bear the cost of covering additional services with no cost sharing, likely passed back to consumers partly through higher premiums.

drawbacks.text: The mandate is unfunded: insurers and employers would absorb the cost of covering additional services free of charge, and much of that cost would likely reappear as higher premiums paid by all enrollees, including people without chronic conditions.
The bill does nothing for uninsured people, who would still pay out of pocket for the same preventive services.

Its scope is deliberately narrow: only items the Secretary certifies as low-cost with strong clinical evidence of cost efficiency would be covered, so many services people might want covered at zero cost sharing would not qualify.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is targeted and evidence-based: waiving small copays on cheap preventive services for people with chronic conditions plausibly avoids much larger downstream costs, and the low-cost requirement limits premium impact. The honest tradeoff is that someone still pays — insurers and employers would pass part of the added coverage cost into premiums, and the narrow scope leaves many chronic-condition patients uncovered. On the whole the design is modest and reasonable, which makes its total inaction notable.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced and sent to an Energy and Commerce health subcommittee, and none of them ever scheduled a hearing or markup, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lauren Underwood introduced the Chronic Condition Copay Elimination Act on July 6, 2021, with Reps. Hayes, Danny K. Davis, and Schakowsky joining as original cosponsors.
The same day, the Speaker referred it to three committees — Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, and Ways and Means — a multi-committee referral that made consideration harder.
It was then referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, where the record ends; no further action, hearing, or vote is listed before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The bill attracted only five Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support in eighteen months.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer health plans kept the status quo: no new mandate to cover chronic-condition preventive care without cost sharing, and no added coverage costs to absorb. Patients who skip preventive care because of copays got no relief.

for.role: Cosponsors, including Reps. Hayes, Danny K. Davis, and Schakowsky

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 6, 2021, sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and never scheduled a hearing or markup.

against.what_they_did: No member sponsored or cosponsored the bill; a coverage mandate without cost sharing had no recorded Republican support.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats (the bill had 5 Democratic cosponsors and none from the other party), and no Republican member of the 117th Congress is recorded as supporting it.

industries.note: The bill would have required insurers to cover additional chronic-condition preventive services with no copays or deductibles, an added coverage cost. Insurers would likely recoup part of it through higher premiums, spreading the cost to all enrollees.
Self-insured employers would directly bear the cost of the new no-cost-sharing mandate. Some could offset it if cheaper preventive care reduces expensive flare-ups and claims later.
Zero-cost preventive visits and screenings would remove a financial barrier that causes patients to skip appointments, bringing more chronic-condition patients into routine care.
